body_en:
## Third quarter: what is "scheme"?

## Preparing for a season

**How a season is prepared under Kyle Shanahan**

Anyone who looks into how an NFL season is planned will quickly find that it is an extremely multilayered process influenced by numerous factors. With Kyle Shanahan and his staff in particular, this process follows a clearly structured approach to make sure the offense is optimally prepared for the coming season.

Every new season begins, as it does for the league's other 31 head coaches, with a comprehensive analysis of the previous one. The staff examines closely which offensive concepts worked and where adjustments are needed. Besides the team's own performance, league-wide developments also play a role, especially which trends are emerging in defensive strategies and whether new tactical approaches are gaining importance. Another central point is a detailed evaluation of the current roster: which players are available? What individual strengths and weaknesses do they bring? And how can the play-calling be best adapted to the available resources?

Based on these findings, Shanahan defines the core principles of the offense for the coming season. The main point is not to hide weaknesses but rather to integrate the players' individual strengths into the system as effectively as possible. A central aspect is the targeted development of individual players so they can reach their full potential. Shanahan's philosophy has mostly been to adapt the system to his key players instead of forcing them into a rigid scheme.

From these findings, a detailed season plan is drawn up that not only defines the overall tactical direction of the offense but also includes targeted options for adjustments over the course of the season. The so-called "**base plays**," fundamental plays that work against various defensive looks, form the backbone. They are complemented by new concepts that are developed further over the season and adapted to the situation. The goal is to establish a clear offensive identity while remaining flexible enough to respond optimally to challenges during the season.

**Real-world examples: successes and challenges**

How this strategy works in practice can be seen in concrete examples from Shanahan's coaching career. A well-known example is the 2012 season, when the then Washington Redskins drafted Robert Griffin III. The decision to take the quarterback was driven primarily by owner Dan Snyder, not by head coach Mike Shanahan. Kyle Shanahan and his assistant at the time, Mike McDaniel, faced the challenge of integrating into their system a player who had played an offense in college that relied heavily on his athletic qualities as a runner, a style that did not fit the Shanahans' classic West Coast offense. To still integrate RGIII successfully, they combined their offense with elements from the college game and introduced numerous read-option plays. Griffin played mostly out of the pistol formation, which gave him simple reads. This revolutionary concept led to him being named Rookie of the Year and took Washington to the playoffs. But the system had a short half-life: Griffin was badly injured and never matched his first-year performances again. The Shanahans also recognized that such an offense is not sustainable in the long run, since defenses would quickly adjust to it, a lesson the 49ers also learned with Colin Kaepernick under Jim Harbaugh and Greg Roman.

Another example of Shanahan's strategic adjustments came in the 2024 season, when he wanted to establish Christian McCaffrey as the central fixture of his offense. After an MVP-worthy 2023 season, the idea was to use McCaffrey not only as a classic running back but increasingly as a receiver against man coverage. This was meant to give Brock Purdy clear reads and create more space for other players. But injuries wrecked that plan. McCaffrey missed most of the season with Achilles and muscle problems and could not return to his previous form in the few games he played. On top of that, other key players went down: rookie Ricky Pearsall was shot, Brandon Aiyuk struggled with his form and later tore his ACL. Without McCaffrey as a reliable option and without receivers who could consistently beat man coverage, the offense struggled. Especially in the red zone, the versatile running back was missing as a matchup weapon, and the 49ers' efficiency there suffered significantly. Despite all of Shanahan's tactical skill, he did not manage to put together a consistent offense.

## Building the game plan

**The importance of game preparation and scouting in the Shanahan offense**

One of Kyle Shanahan's greatest strengths as a play-caller is his meticulous game preparation, based on a detailed analysis of the opposing defense. His offensive system is characterized not only by sophisticated play designs but also by targeted strategic planning aimed at consistently exploiting weaknesses in the opposing defense. Three central factors play a decisive role: identifying defensive weak spots, manipulating the defense through pre-snap motion and a wide variety of formations, and flexibly adapting the game plan to the team's own personnel.

The first step in game preparation is a comprehensive analysis of the opposing defense. Shanahan and his staff go through extensive video material and identify specific patterns and tendencies. The focus is particularly on the opposing defense's preferred coverage structures: is it primarily man or zone coverage? How do the linebackers react to play-action fakes, and are they prone to taking bad angles? Are there individual defenders who struggle with certain concepts or misdirection? And last but not least: how do the safeties position themselves when there is movement in the backfield, and can that open up space for deep passes? This detailed scouting work allows Shanahan to develop tailor-made game plans that specifically attack the weaknesses of each defense.

Another central element of his offense is the consistent use of pre-snap motion and variable formations. These serve not only to throw the defense off balance but also to decode the defensive strategy early. Targeted movement before the snap pulls defenders out of their assigned positions to create mismatches and destabilize defensive structures. At the same time, it allows the quarterback to gather information about the defense's coverage before the snap, for instance whether the defense is playing man or zone coverage. This constant movement also causes confusion, since defensive responsibilities change around the snap and communication problems can arise. A classic example of this strategy is the use of "jet motion," in which a receiver runs across the field before the snap. This forces the defense to react immediately and can either open gaps in the run game or shift the coverage in a way that creates passing windows. Players like George Kittle, Kyle Juszczyk, Deebo Samuel or McCaffrey make life hard for opposing defenses simply because they can, in principle, line up at any position outside the offensive line. That makes it very hard for defensive play-callers to anticipate the next play from the personnel on the field and respond with the right defensive call.

Besides analyzing the opposing defense, another central part of Shanahan's strategy is adapting the offensive system to the individual strengths of his own players. His system does not follow a rigid philosophy but is flexibly designed to use the available personnel optimally. If a wide receiver has a particular strength against a certain coverage, the play design is tailored to put him in that favorable situation. The quarterback's role is optimized accordingly as well: while a distributor like Brock Purdy works with quick, rhythmic passes, a more mobile quarterback is involved more heavily in bootlegs and play-action rollouts. This adaptability is especially evident in the run game: since the running game is a central part of his offense, Shanahan varies the blocking schemes between inside zone, outside zone and gap schemes, depending on the strengths of the offensive line.

All these elements make Shanahan's offense one of the most varied and at the same time most effective in the NFL. The combination of in-depth analysis, tactical manipulation of the defense and flexible adaptation to his own personnel ensures that his offense ranks among the most productive in the league year after year, regardless of opponent, quarterback or available playmakers.

## Play-calling during a game

Kyle Shanahan is considered one of the most creative play-callers in the NFL. His offense follows a clear structure but remains hard for defenses to predict, because it is based on several fundamental principles. These principles make it extremely difficult for defenses to adjust to his plays and develop effective countermeasures. Three central aspects shape his play-calling in particular: linking plays together, deliberately turning a defense's own rules against it, and maximizing yards after the catch (YAC) from his physically above-average players.

A central feature of the Shanahan offense is the way different plays are linked to each other, a concept known as "**tying plays together**." Many of his designs look identical at first glance but have completely different points of attack, forcing the defense to react on suspicion. A classic example is the outside zone run game, where the formation before the snap looks identical but, depending on the call, a play-action pass or a bootleg can come out of it as well. Both the offensive line and the quarterback make the same movements at the start, so linebackers and safeties can only recognize at the last moment what is really happening. The result: a moment of hesitation is often enough to allow big gains. Since every play could be a potential continuation or variation of an earlier one, defenses are under constant pressure to make quick decisions, with a high probability of mistakes.

Another decisive aspect is Shanahan's ability to use a defense's basic principles against it. His play designs regularly put defenders in dilemmas where there is no optimal decision. Linebackers who hold their position to stop the run risk being outmaneuvered in the passing game. Defenders who crash forward too aggressively against the run leave open space at the second level, which Shanahan attacks specifically with crossing routes, leak concepts or delayed routes by tight ends. The defense is thus forced to react to movement instead of actively controlling the game, one reason why Shanahan's offense so often creates open passing options so effortlessly. In other situations, Shanahan exploits instinctive movements by defenders that he noticed during tape study; with a double move, for example, he can send an overaggressive defender down the wrong path and create an open throw for his QB.

The third cornerstone of his philosophy is maximizing yards after the catch (YAC). While many offensive systems rely on receivers making spectacular catches in tight windows, Shanahan focuses on putting his playmakers, all of whom have strong physical tools, in optimal situations after the catch. His system is based on putting defenses in motion and thus creating space in which players can gain as many yards as possible after the catch. Especially in combination with tying plays together, new opportunities to outplay defenses keep arising over the course of a game. As soon as a defender's movement is spotted on tape that can be exploited, the next play design is built on it to attack exactly that weak spot.

This consistent focus on YAC is one of the main reasons why Shanahan's offense remains highly efficient even with quarterbacks who are not part of the absolute elite. Instead of forcing complicated vertical throws, he creates a system that allows his players to make the difference after the catch. The combination of perfectly coordinated plays, targeted manipulation of the defense and maximizing gains after the catch makes Shanahan's offense one of the most innovative and effective in the NFL.

But what impact does the scheme have on the quarterbacks? Are they better or worse than the rest, or could you put a Division II QB in there and get similar numbers? The final quarter should shed light on that: fourth quarter, Shanahan and his quarterbacks.
